extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students of mathematical analysis and differential equations (French-speaking)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methods for (1) reducing and integrating systems of differential equations and first-order partial differential equations via integrals premières and characteristic/generatrix curves, and (2) elementary numerical approximation of definite integrals (trapezoidal, Simpson, Dupuit roulette).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of higher-order systems to first-order systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Si l'on a à intégrer un système de n équations d'ordres divers à n fonctions inconnues, on le ramène à un système d'équations du premier ordre en prenant pour inconnues auxiliaires les dérivées successives des fonctions inconnues primitives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce auxiliary unknowns equal to successive derivatives (example: three second-order equations for x,y,z → six first-order equations for x,y,z,x',y',z'). The resulting first-order system can be integrated when initial values of all auxiliary functions at t0 are known; this corresponds mechanically to specifying initial positions and velocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of integrales premières to lower system order
rubrics_metrics.description: La connaissance de chaque intégrale première nouvelle sert à abaisser d'une unité le nombre des fonctions inconnues; si on connaît n intégrales premières, le système est intégré.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find first integrals (relations among variables and derivatives equal to constants) and substitute to reduce the number of unknown functions. Example: two first integrals allow lowering unknowns by two and reduce to quadratures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and nature of first-order PDEs
rubrics_metrics.description: Une équation aux dérivées partielles du premier ordre, à deux variables indépendantes x et y, est une équation de la forme F(x,y,z,p,q)=0, où p=∂z/∂x et q=∂z/∂y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrating such an equation means finding all surfaces z(x,y) that satisfy it. The general integral contains an arbitrary function (not a mere constant): the arbitrary function must be chosen so the integral surface can be made to pass through a prescribed curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming PDEs from families of surfaces with arbitrary constants
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a family of surfaces determined by relations that depend on arbitrary constants C1,C2 (generatrices), and a condition F(C1,C2)=0 fixing a director curve, eliminate the constants between these relations to obtain the surface equation F(...)=0; from this process one can derive a PDE independent of the particular arbitrary function F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: write equations of generators involving C1,C2, differentiate to express p and q, then eliminate C1,C2 (and sometimes their ratios) to obtain a PDE that all surfaces in the family satisfy. Geometrically this PDE often expresses that the tangent plane contains the generator tangent.

rubrics_metrics.name: PDE of cylindrical surfaces (generators parallel to a fixed direction)
rubrics_metrics.description: All cylindrical surfaces whose generatrices have a given direction satisfy a linear first-order PDE of the form a p + b q = c (derived from F(az - ex, bz - cy)=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: set u = az - ex, v = bz - cy, express p and q from derivatives of F(u,v), eliminate F to get relation ap + bq = c. Geometric interpretation: the tangent plane at each point contains the generating line (its tangent).

rubrics_metrics.name: PDE of conical surfaces (generators through the origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surfaces generated by lines through the origin (cones with vertex at 0) have a general equation F(x/y, x/z, ...) leading to a first-order PDE (text denoted as equation (8)) which expresses that the tangent plane contains the tangent to the generator through the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: write generator equations with constants, impose condition F(C1,C2)=0, eliminate constants to get the cone equation. Geometric meaning: in each point M the tangent plane contains the tangent along the generator (line through origin).

rubrics_metrics.name: PDE of surfaces of revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Surfaces of revolution about an axis, obtained by moving a generating curve (circle) whose parameters are constrained by a director, yield a first-order PDE (given in the text) expressing that the tangent plane contains the tangent to the generator curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parameterize the generator (e.g., circle with constants), eliminate parameters using the director condition to obtain the PDE. The PDE can be written in terms of combinations like x^2+y^2 and leads to relations between p and q; geometrically the tangent plane contains the tangent to the generating circle at each point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric interpretation of linear first-order PDEs (segment MA tangent condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear PDE of the form A(x,y,z) p + B(x,y,z) q = C(x,y,z) can be interpreted by associating to each point M a segment MA with projections A(x,y,z), B(x,y,z), C(x,y,z); the PDE holds for surfaces S for which, at each point M, the corresponding segment MA is tangent to S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the segment MA with components given by the PDE coefficients; require MA to lie in the tangent plane z - z0 = p (x - x0) + q (y - y0). This yields the PDE. Integration then reduces to finding curves whose tangent coincides with MA (characteristic/generatrix curves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of characteristics / generating curves for first-order PDEs
rubrics_metrics.description: To integrate A p + B q = C, find curves (generatrices) whose tangent at each point coincides with the segment MA, i.e., solve the ODE system dx / A = dy / B = dz / C. Integrate to obtain two constants C1,C2; the general integral surfaces are given by F(C1,C2)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) write the differential equations of generating curves: dx : dy : dz = A : B : C; (2) integrate to obtain two independent first integrals (constants); (3) solve these for C1,C2 and eliminate them by imposing an arbitrary relation F(C1,C2)=0 to get the integral surface. If the prescribed curve is itself a generator, exceptional multiplicity of integral surfaces occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional case when prescribed curve is a generator
rubrics_metrics.description: If the curve by which the integral surface is to pass is itself one of the generating curves (a génératrice), there exists an infinity of integral surfaces passing through that curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: moving the generating curve continuously produces infinitely many surfaces containing that given generator; thus prescribing a single generator does not determine a unique integral surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear first-order PDEs in p and q: integration algorithm summary
rubrics_metrics.description: For linear PDE pf(x,y,z)+q g(x,y,z)=h(x,y,z), integrate by finding families of characteristic curves whose differential equations are dx / f = dy / g = dz / h; integrate to obtain two constants and form the integral surface F(C1,C2)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text frames this via the segment MA construction: the coefficients f,g,h are the projections of MA. Solve the characteristics, express their general solution with two arbitrary constants, then eliminate to get the surface family. This yields all integral surfaces; choosing F fixes a particular integral passing through a director curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order PDEs general solution behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: A second-order PDE in x and y has a most general solution depending on two arbitrary functions. Specifying a curve and the law of tangent planes along that curve determines a unique solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example treated: surfaces with zero total curvature satisfy a PDE (equation (13)); integrating shows solutions are developable surfaces. The criterion 'p is a function of q' (or vice versa) implies that the tangent plane equations depend on a single parameter and thus the surface is an envelope of a one-parameter family of planes (developable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trapezoidal rule for numerical integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate the area under y=f(x) between a and b by subdividing [a,b] into n equal subintervals of width h and replacing the curve by the inscribed polygon, giving the trapezoidal sum: (h/2)[y0 + y_n + 2(sum_{i=1}^{n-1} y_i)].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy improves as n increases. Use equidistant ordinates for the simple trapezoidal formula. This is the basic quadrature method for approximating definite integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dupuit roulette method for area measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical device: use a Dupuit wheel (two geared graduated wheels) and a transparent paper with parallel equally spaced lines to approximate area of a closed contour by summing lengths of intersections and multiplying by spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: lay transparent grid so two grid lines are tangent to contour ends, read sum of lengths of intersections by rolling the wheel along each grid line; multiply sum by spacing to get area estimate. Tip: place grid so angular points fall on grid lines when possible to improve accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simpson's rule for numerical integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide interval into an even number 2p of equal parts and, over each pair of subintervals, fit a vertical-axis parabola through three consecutive points; sum areas of these parabolic segments to approximate the integral. The local parabolic area formula yields Simpson's composite rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires an even number of subintervals. For each group of two intervals with spacing h, the area contribution is (h/3)[y_{i} + 4 y_{i+1} + y_{i+2}] (leading to the standard composite Simpson formula when summed). Use careful plotting and measurement (Dupuit wheel) to evaluate sums when needed.
